en: Was what fate imposed upon you fulfilled,
There was no black one who would flee,
There was no manly youth to grapple with him,
When my father Erdi died,
When the multitude fell away,
At that time, Akkanoshu,
His company took to the road of [?],
I myself was still in childhood,
Until I reached eleven years of age,
Orphaned, I endured hardship,
When I grew from twelve to sixteen,
I entered the age of manhood,
When I passed from seventeen to sixteen,
I entered the realm of death,
When I reached seventeen,
Such were those bygone days.
How many households belong to Tobo,
If you leave my camp, my precious one,
If there is an enemy with a mouth like an ember,
If the foe you confront should come.
Showing solitary might,
Glittering upon the mountain pass,
The collared one was Khan Kurai,
My father Boruk was a hero,
There is death beyond dying,
Born fiercer than mankind.
To the fire, the spirit of my forefather,
To rise and charge once,
Hundreds passed and people departed,
The late Jai-Janybek,
Departed alive from among them,
Erik Kyz’s marvel,
Crushed, with sorrow welling up,
With Jeti, the son of Kokot,
Spreading densely across the land without restraint,
A living, rather small one,
Unable to match your strength,
Driving away his people and kin,
Going without sparing his people’s feast,
Gathering his people and making war,
My greeting that lies cherished.
My people, like starlings,
The hero whom others regarded as an equal.
Who brought them to Aizapar,
Praised at a thousand feasts,
Among the souls with crimson steeds.
The khan who led the people,
Making his assembled people march,
Sending various caravans across,
My inexhaustible radiant fortune,
Separately, to the hero Kurman,
His forehead rises prominently,
His forehead bone is ridged,
It flows down his back,
It flows from his waist,
His aspect is dark and fearsome,
Born of Er Chongtai,
Looking toward the sun,
Forty pack camels for the campaign,
Asking whether forty hungry camels exist,
The champion of the countless multitude,
The might of the teeming multitude,
The remnant that knew no spring,
The valiant one in the city of Kaina,
The two peoples, Turkmen and Joomun,
Of the Kalmyks in many ranks,
He broke through and took [?],
The one who devastated [?],
He stirred his prowess,
He scattered them from Tostokan,
Of the silk that carried the load,
The looming [?],
The four Alash peoples joined together,
The Tengri-faithful [?],
Extinguishing your blazing fire,
Turn your own smoke-pipe,
Taking [?] and drawing the bow,
Casting away your ornaments,
Your Kalmyk fit to mount a horse,
When exhausted, even a poor horse,
You will surely let it go without fighting,
You drove yourself away from the livestock,
My paradisal, prosperous days,
Shedding blood for my queen-mother,
Left humbled among the Kokand people,
Oh, the condition of the [?] enemy,
Making an Oghuz dwelling of his bull,
Calling Tündübai my people,
They plundered all his possessions,
The heroes overran his settlement,
They boldly joined battle against the enemy,
The hero's son Keneshe,
However much he remained unbroken, however much [?],
The wrestler remained unbroken and tireless,
Taking offense, yet not quarreling,
Without disputing over their livestock and goods,
My father goes toward Kongur,
Two friends born as brothers,
He rides his horse toward Kongur,
Bakay sets out to search,
He comes forth destroying households,
He sent the girl away unharmed,
Saying he should pull from the side of the threshold,
Keneshe seems like Rozan,
The wind of that wretched fellow,
One who traveled through the night was his equal,
One of the capped men's [?],
After hearing the news,
After the forest heard and scattered,
He surpassed the devastation,
He lived on after ravaging the people,
He witnessed black treachery,
Hearing a great deal of gossip,
Tomorrow, to the abode of Judgment Day,
They fought, saying that tribute had been imposed,
His body was as massive as a house,
Then afterward behold his prize,
Breaking it, he burned with anguish,
Humiliated from over there,
Being thwarted in every undertaking,
Whatever he does, from my wind,
My God knows the thought with which I went
Taking many from the Kyrgyz
